title: Does Earl Grey Tea Have Caffeine? (Black Tea + Bergamot)
h1: Does earl grey tea have caffeine?
meta_description: Yes — Earl Grey has caffeine from its black tea base (site range 40–70 mg/cup; WebMD reports 40–120 mg). Bergamot adds flavor, not caffeine.

body_html:
Yes — Earl Grey has caffeine, and it comes entirely from its black tea base. This site's working range for black tea is 40–70 mg per 8 oz cup (avg ~50 mg); WebMD reports a wider published figure specifically for Earl Grey of 40 to 120 milligrams per cup. Bergamot, the citrus oil that gives Earl Grey its signature flavor, doesn't add or remove any of it.

How much caffeine is in Earl Grey tea?

Per WebMD, “your cup of Earl Grey tea also contains 40 to 120 milligrams of caffeine.” That's a wide published band, and it's wider than this site's general black-tea range (40–70 mg) — a difference that likely reflects how strongly a given Earl Grey is brewed and how heavily the bergamot-oil coating covers the leaf, rather than a different plant or process. Other sources on black tea generally show similar spread: Medical News Today puts black tea at 64–112 mg per 8 fl oz, while the FDA's figure of 71 mg per 12 oz works out to about 47 mg per 8 oz. Published black-tea numbers vary meaningfully by source and method — there isn't one single agreed-upon figure, for Earl Grey or for black tea generally.

What is Earl Grey tea?

Earl Grey is a flavored black tea, not a distinct tea type of its own. WebMD describes it plainly: “Traditionally, it's a simple blend of black tea and oil of bergamot,” bergamot being a bitter citrus fruit grown mainly in southern Italy. The black tea leaf supplies the caffeine, body, and tannins; the bergamot oil supplies the citrusy, floral aroma Earl Grey is known for. Some modern versions swap in green tea, oolong, or rooibos as the base and still call the result “Earl Grey” because of the bergamot flavoring — which means the caffeine range on this page applies to traditional, black-tea-based Earl Grey specifically, and a rooibos-based “Earl Grey” would be caffeine-free instead.

Does bergamot add caffeine?

No. Caffeine is a compound the tea plant (Camellia sinensis) produces in its leaves; bergamot is an unrelated citrus fruit used only for its oil's aroma. Flavoring a black tea with bergamot changes how it tastes and smells — it doesn't add, remove, or otherwise change the caffeine already present in the tea leaf underneath.

Earl Grey vs. black tea vs. other drinks, compared

Use the calculator above to compare Earl Grey's black-tea base against any other drink, by the cup or across a full day, or check the static reference table below:

DrinkServingTypical caffeineRange
Earl Grey tea (published range, WebMD)8 oz—40–120 mg
Black tea (steeped — Earl Grey's base)8 oz~50 mg40–70 mg
White tea (steeped)8 oz~25 mg15–30 mg
Green tea (steeped)8 oz~35 mg30–50 mg
Matcha1 tsp (2 g) whisked in 2–3 oz~65–70 mg60–80 mg
Espresso1 oz shot~63 mg60–80 mg
Brewed coffee8 oz~95 mg80–100 mg
Rooibos / herbal (caffeine-free)8 oz0 mgcaffeine-free

Even at its published high end (120 mg), a strong cup of Earl Grey can approach brewed coffee's typical range — but at the low end (40 mg), it's closer to a light green tea. The spread is wide enough that “how strong did you brew it” matters more for Earl Grey than for most single-origin teas.

What changes Earl Grey's caffeine

  • Steep time and water temperature. A longer steep in hotter water pulls more caffeine from the black tea leaf underneath the bergamot coating.
  • Leaf-to-water ratio. More tea per cup means a stronger, more caffeinated brew.
  • How the bergamot is applied. A tea scented with natural bergamot rind or herbs tends to be milder than one coated in concentrated bergamot oil, but this affects flavor intensity, not the caffeine coming from the tea leaf itself.
  • Base tea substitution. An Earl Grey made with green tea, oolong, or rooibos instead of black tea will carry that base's caffeine range instead — always check the ingredient list if the base matters to you.

Is there a caffeine-free Earl Grey?

A traditional black-tea Earl Grey is not caffeine-free. Two lower-caffeine options exist instead: decaf Earl Grey, made by decaffeinating the black tea base — Medical News Today notes that “decaffeinated varieties of popular teas are usually available,” including Earl Grey — and rooibos-based “Earl Grey,” which swaps in caffeine-free rooibos and keeps only the bergamot flavoring. Decaffeination is worth a caveat: it removes most, not all, of a tea's caffeine, so a decaf Earl Grey still carries a small residual amount rather than being truly 0 mg.

Is Earl Grey's caffeine a lot?

Earl Grey's black-tea-range caffeine (roughly 40–70 mg on this site's figures, up to a published 120 mg on the high end) is a meaningful but not extreme share of the general daily reference the U.S. FDA has cited — about 400 mg per day as a level not generally associated with negative effects for most healthy adults. That reference covers everything caffeinated you drink in a day, not any single cup. People who are pregnant, caffeine-sensitive, or managing a health condition should talk to a healthcare provider about what caffeine level is appropriate for them.

For the full black-tea breakdown Earl Grey's base draws from, see black tea: caffeine and the evidence. For how Earl Grey compares to chai, another black-tea-based blend, see chai caffeine.

This describes published research and general information, not medical or dietary advice.

faqs.q: Does Earl Grey tea have caffeine?
faqs.a: Yes. Earl Grey is black tea flavored with bergamot, so its caffeine comes from the black tea base. This site's working range is 40–70 mg per 8 oz cup; WebMD reports a wider published figure of 40–120 mg.

faqs.q: How much caffeine is in Earl Grey tea?
faqs.a: WebMD reports 40 to 120 milligrams per cup. Published black-tea figures vary by source — Medical News Today puts black tea at 64–112 mg per 8 fl oz, while the FDA's 71 mg per 12 oz works out to about 47 mg per 8 oz.

faqs.q: Does bergamot add caffeine to Earl Grey?
faqs.a: No. Bergamot is a citrus fruit used only for its oil's aroma. All of Earl Grey's caffeine comes from the black tea leaf underneath; bergamot doesn't add, remove, or change it.

faqs.q: Is Earl Grey more caffeinated than regular black tea?
faqs.a: Not inherently — Earl Grey is black tea, just flavored with bergamot. Published Earl Grey figures (40–120 mg) run somewhat wider than this site's general black-tea range (40–70 mg), which likely reflects brew strength rather than the bergamot itself.

faqs.q: Is there a caffeine-free Earl Grey?
faqs.a: A traditional black-tea Earl Grey is not caffeine-free. Decaf Earl Grey and rooibos-based 'Earl Grey' (bergamot-flavored rooibos) are the two lower- or no-caffeine alternatives.

faqs.q: Is decaf Earl Grey really caffeine-free?
faqs.a: Not completely. Decaffeination removes most of a tea's caffeine but not all of it, so decaf Earl Grey carries a small residual amount rather than a true 0 mg.

faqs.q: Does Earl Grey have less caffeine than coffee?
faqs.a: Usually yes — this site's typical range (40–70 mg) is well below brewed coffee's 80–100 mg per 8 oz. At the published high end (120 mg), a strong cup can approach coffee's range.
It's a moderate-to-high true tea, in line with black tea generally — more caffeine than green or white tea, less than a shot of espresso or a cup of brewed coffee on average.

faqs.q: What kind of tea is Earl Grey made from?
faqs.a: Traditionally, black tea flavored with oil of bergamot. Some modern versions substitute green tea, oolong, or rooibos as the base, which changes the caffeine range accordingly.

faqs.q: Does the strength of Earl Grey change how much caffeine it has?
faqs.a: Yes — steep time, water temperature, and leaf-to-water ratio all move the number, which is a large part of why published Earl Grey figures span such a wide range (40–120 mg).

faqs.q: Does Earl Grey have more caffeine than green tea?
faqs.a: Generally yes. Earl Grey's black-tea base (40–70 mg typical) runs above green tea's typical range (30–50 mg).
